newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- FEB 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- FEB 5.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--Greece is again facing the prospect of being cutting in two by farmers blockading national roads as a strong police force deployed in the Thessaly region has shown itself to be less than effective at deterring them. In a game of guerrilla cat and mouse, the farmers have so far won the war of impressions and proclaimed that they can "cut the country in two whenever we want".

--The tax department and local government are forging an alliance in the face of drivers refusing to pay fines levied for road violations or parking. A new legislative amendment jointly promoted by the interior and finance ministries will ensure that outstanding fines are deducted from tax declarations.

--Striking high school teachers are hardening their stance, rejecting the latest compromise proposal to wind down protests in their three-week strike. Primary school teachers, meanwhile, look set to declare another five-day extension to their strike, effectively shutting down all state schools. Education Minister Gerasimos Arsenis is seeking a way out of the impasse by looking at whether EU funds lying dormant for the last three years can be used.

--The national economy ministry is building up steam to push forward the government's privatisation policy. National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou has already received an expert study on a two-year timeframe to get the programme going again.

--Farmers win the first battle of the Thessaly road war: the region appears to have become a gigantic chess game. Farmers appear determined to continue the game while the unwilling player - the government - insists that it has given all it can.

--Development Minister Vasso Papandreou has sent a 17-page document to parliament's fact-finding commission on the Floisvos casino licence. The document is alleged to definitively prove the guilt of the former tourism minister who approved the contract for the casino.

--Vasso Papandreou's document alleges that the casino contract was signed over to a consortium that had not been exhaustively checked by the competent authorities, and laying blame on a Supreme Court deputy president heading the committee on the casino.
--A series of commemorative stamps on Andreas Papandreou, the founder and late president of ruling party PASOK, will be issued on February 12.
--The interior ministry announced yesterday that it would seek to employee 12,750 new civil servants in municipalities and prefectural authorities, on both a seasonal and permanent basis.
--The farmers showed yesterday who controlled the country's national roads. They do.

--Parents have appealed to teachers and government to do something quickly about the situation in the education sector which has seen high schools shut for the past three weeks. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
